Question Choices: Select. Two animals have different masses, but their masses are not given. Can comparing only the numbers 2/5 and 3/5 tell us which has greater mass: 2/5 of the first animal or 3/5 of the second? ~~Yes | No~~
Hints: You can compare the fraction numbers. To compare the resulting masses, you also need information about the whole masses.
Solution: No. The number 2/5 is less than 3/5, but the portions use different whole masses. If the animals have masses 10 kg and 20 kg, the portions are 4 kg and 12 kg. If they have masses 30 kg and 10 kg, the portions are 12 kg and 6 kg. Either portion can be heavier. Fractions of different wholes can be compared when enough information about the wholes is known.

Question Choices: Amy ate 3/5 of the length of a short candy strip. Nikko ate 3/5 of the length of a longer candy strip. Who ate a greater length of candy?
Hints: The same positive fraction of a longer length is longer.
Solution: Nikko. Both eat three fifths of their own strip lengths. Multiplying the larger starting length by the same positive fraction gives the larger eaten length. This conclusion compares length, not mass or volume.

Question Choices: Select, You ate 2/7 of a large pizza. Your friend ate 2/7 of a small pizza. Who ate more? ~~You | Your-friend~~
Solution: You. Both portions are 2/7 of their own pizza, but your whole pizza is larger. The same positive fraction of the larger whole gives more pizza.

Question Choices: Select. Both stores sell the same toy car and use the same regular price. Store A charges 6/7 of that price; Store B charges 5/7. Which store is cheaper? ~~Store-A | Store-B~~
Hints: For the same whole or equal-sized wholes, equal denominators mean equal-sized pieces. Compare the numerators.
Solution: Both stores use the same regular price. Compare the fractions: 5/7 < 6/7 because 5 < 6. Store B charges the smaller fraction of the same price, so select Store-B.

Question Choices: Put the fractions in order from largest to smallest: 13/15, 13/10, 13/18
Hints: For the same whole or equal-sized wholes, a larger positive denominator means smaller pieces. Compare the same positive number of those pieces.
Solution: The numerator is 13 throughout. Tenths are larger than fifteenths, which are larger than eighteenths. Descending order: 13/10, 13/15, 13/18.

Question Choices: Select, Student A and student B both ran for 1/3 of an hour. Who ran longer time? ~~The-same | Student-A | Student-B~~
Solution: The-same. Both durations are 1/3 of the same time unit, an hour. Since 60 divided by 3 = 20, each ran for 20 minutes.

Question Choices: Each friend has a pizza of the same size. Emma ate 2/8 of her pizza, Liam ate 5/8 of his pizza, and Noah ate 3/8 of his pizza. Who ate the most pizza?
Hints: For the same whole or equal-sized wholes, equal denominators mean equal-sized pieces. Compare the numerators.
Solution: The pizzas are equal-sized and the fractions all count eighths. Since 5 is greater than 3 and 2, Liam ate the most: 5/8.

Question Choices: Select. Can 2/9 of a long rope be longer than 2/5 of a short rope? ~~Yes | No~~
Solution: Yes. For example, take a long rope of 45 metres and a short rope of 5 metres. Then 2/9 of 45 is 10 metres, while 2/5 of 5 is 2 metres. The portion of the long rope is longer even though 2/9 < 2/5.

Question Choices: Select, Which is larger? 3/4 of a smaller cake or 1/3 of a larger cake? ~~3/4-smaller-cake | 1/3-larger-cake | Cannot-tell~~
Hints: Do we know the exact sizes?
Solution: Cannot-tell. For example, if the cakes weigh 4 and 6 units, the portions weigh 3 and 2, so the smaller-cake portion is larger. If the cakes weigh 4 and 12 units, the portions weigh 3 and 4, reversing the result. Actual whole sizes are needed.
